# What Is Value-Based Pricing?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-value-based-pricing/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-10 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Value-based pricing sets a price from the value an offer creates for a defined buyer, measured against that buyer's next best alternative. Pricing research treats it as the strongest approach and finds it the least used. The difficulty is less the arithmetic than measuring value, segmenting by it and holding the price once sellers start to negotiate.

Value-based pricing sets a price from the value an offer creates for a specific buyer, measured against that buyer's next best alternative, rather than from the seller's cost or a competitor's list price. Pricing researchers generally rank it as the strongest of the three main approaches, and the evidence says it is the least used. The arithmetic is simple. The hard parts are measuring value with real customer data and holding the price once a negotiation starts.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

## What value-based pricing means

Most firms set price in one of three ways. Hinterhuber's review, published in the *Journal of Business Strategy*, averaged nearly two dozen studies of pricing practice across the US, Europe and Asia.

| Approach | Starting point | Share of firms in Hinterhuber's review | Main weakness |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cost-based | Cost plus a target margin | 37% | Ignores what the buyer would pay |
| Competition-based | Competitors' prices | 44% | Ignores how the offer differs |
| Customer value-based | Value to the buyer against the next best alternative | 17% | Needs customer data that is hard to collect |

Value-based pricing does not mean charging the full value. Cost sets the floor. The buyer's estimate of value sets the ceiling. The price sits between them, and the share of value left with the buyer is their reason to choose you. For a services firm the next best alternative may be an internal team, a competitor or doing nothing.

## How it works

The method has four steps: name the alternative, list the differences, put a money value on each, and choose where in the band to price. Hinterhuber and Liozu's article in *MIT Sloan Management Review* gives a worked case from a European supermarket chain pricing a private-label yogurt.

| Step | Figure in the published case |
| --- | --- |
| Cost of goods | €1.29 |
| Original price | €1.99 |
| Next best alternative: branded yogurt | €2.99 |
| Value of added health benefit | about +€0.30 |
| Penalty for no brand name | about −€0.50 |
| Estimated perceived value | about €2.80 |
| Recommended price, after testing price sensitivity and competitor reaction | €2.49 |

The authors report that sales beat volume targets at the higher price and profits were nearly six times the plan. It is one consumer case, reported by its authors. In business markets the differences are usually money the buyer saves or earns.

In B2B, the value estimate should come from customers, not from the seller's slide. Anderson and Narus proposed customer value models built mainly through field value assessments, either for one customer or for a segment. Expert interviews, buyer workshops and conjoint analysis are the usual tools, and [Pricing Experiments in B2B](https://lowob.com/research/pricing-experiments-in-b2b/) covers how to test a price once it is set.

## Why it matters for a commercial team

Value-based pricing sets the list price within a [pricing architecture](https://lowob.com/research/pricing-architecture-for-services-firms/). It fails most often after the price is set.

Hinterhuber's workshops with executives at nine companies identified six obstacles. Two sit in the commercial team: segmenting customers by need, and sales force management, where unnecessary discounts cause "value leakage". The remedies he describes are clear discount authority, pay, training and monitoring. That is the subject of [Discount Governance](https://lowob.com/research/discount-governance/).

Realisation is the wider problem. Simon-Kucher's 2025 Global Pricing Study, covering 28 countries and 39 industries, found firms keep less than half of the price increases they announce. A value-based list price that sellers discount back to the competitor's level is competition-based pricing with extra work.

Value-based pricing also shapes the value metric. If value appears per completed task, a seat price under-charges; [Seats, Usage or Outcomes](https://lowob.com/research/seats-usage-or-outcomes/) covers that choice.

> Cost sets the floor and value sets the ceiling. The gap between price and value is the buyer's reason to sign.

## How to start

| Test | Question to answer | Warning sign |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Alternative | What would this buyer do if you did not exist? | "There is no alternative" |
| Differences | Which two or three differences matter most to the buyer, in money? | A feature list with no figures |
| Evidence | Where did each value figure come from? | Only internal estimates |
| Segment | Does value differ enough by segment to justify different offers? | One price for every buyer |
| Realisation | What did you actually collect on the last ten deals? | Nobody knows |
| Record | Who owns the value estimate, and when is it checked? | It lives in one person's head |

In **lowob**'s model a price is a commercial decision like any other. It belongs in the record with its reason, the value estimate behind it, its owner, the expected result and a check date. An agent can draft the value case from call notes and CRM history at autonomy level 1. The price itself stays with a person.

## lowob takeaways

- **Start from the alternative.** Value is always measured against what the buyer would otherwise do.
- **Use customer evidence.** Value figures from field interviews hold up in negotiation; internal estimates do not.
- **Protect realisation.** A value-based list price only matters if discount rules hold it.
- **Record the estimate.** The reason behind a price is what lets the next price improve.

## Sources and notes

- [Management and Accounting Web, summary of Hinterhuber, "Customer value-based pricing strategies: why companies resist", Journal of Business Strategy 29(4)](https://maaw.info/ArticleSummaries/ArtSumHinterhuber2008.htm), 2008. Academic summary of a review of 1983 to 2006 studies; shares are averages across differing surveys.
- [Hinterhuber and Liozu, Setting Prices Based on Customer Value, MIT Sloan Management Review](https://sloanreview.mit.edu/article/setting-prices-based-on-customer-value), 2012. Excerpt from an academic article; the yogurt case is a single example reported by the authors.
- [Management and Accounting Web, summary of Hinterhuber and Liozu (2012)](https://maaw.info/ArticleSummaries/ArtSumHinterhuberLiozu2012.htm). Academic summary; interview study of 15 US industrial firms, small sample.
- [Kellogg School of Management, Anderson and Narus, Business Marketing: Understand What Customers Value](https://www.kellogg.northwestern.edu/faculty/research/detail/1998/business-marketing-understand-what-customers-value), Harvard Business Review, 1998. Abstract page only; older work on method, not measured outcomes.
- [Simon-Kucher, The State of Pricing 2025: Global Pricing Study](https://www.simon-kucher.com/en/insights/global-pricing-study), 2025. Consultancy survey of 2,200+ leaders; realisation figure is self-reported.
